sections.title: 8.1 Lattice Concepts
sections.summary: Bases, volume, Gram-Schmidt, LLL reduction implemented and verified exactly, Babai decoding with good and bad bases, and how close LLL gets to the shortest vector.

blocks.markdown:
A **lattice** is the set of all integer combinations of linearly independent vectors b1, ..., bd, called a **basis**. A lattice has infinitely many bases: two bases describe the same lattice exactly when they differ by a **unimodular** integer matrix (determinant ±1), and the **volume** |det B| is the same for all of them (B07, Nakamura and Yasuda, section 2.1). The **Gram-Schmidt** vectors turn a basis into orthogonal ones, and the volume equals the product of their lengths. A basis is *good* when its vectors are short and nearly orthogonal and *bad* when they are long and nearly parallel; the same lattice can be given either way.

Two problems matter for cryptography (B07, section 2.2). The **shortest vector problem (SVP)** asks for a shortest non-zero lattice vector, of length λ1; it is NP-hard under randomised reductions. The **closest vector problem (CVP)** asks for the lattice point nearest to a target. Both are easy given a good basis and believed hard given a bad one, which is the design idea behind lattice cryptography. For a random lattice the **Gaussian heuristic** predicts λ1 ≈ sqrt(d/(2πe)) · vol^(1/d). The **LLL algorithm** turns any basis into a reduced one in polynomial time: it is *size-reduced* (|μij| ≤ 1/2) and satisfies the **Lovász condition** between neighbouring Gram-Schmidt vectors; its first vector is at most (1/(δ − 1/4))^((d−1)/4) · vol^(1/d). The strength of LLL is far better in practice than that bound, but it is still exponentially far from the shortest vector in high dimension, and this gap is what the security of lattice schemes rests on.

The first listing implements LLL with floating-point Gram-Schmidt and then **verifies the result exactly with rational arithmetic**, so the checker does not trust the floating-point code. It shows the same two-dimensional lattice described by two bases, and then **Babai's nearest-plane decoding** in dimension 12 with a good basis, a bad basis and the LLL-reduced bad basis. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

import math, random
import numpy as np
from fractions import Fraction

def lll(basis, delta=0.99):
    B = np.array(basis, dtype=np.int64)
    n = len(B)
    Bs = np.zeros((n, B.shape[1])); mu = np.zeros((n, n)); nrm = np.zeros(n)
    valid = 0
    def gram_schmidt_row(i):
        v = B[i].astype(float)
        for j in range(i):
            mu[i, j] = (B[i] @ Bs[j]) / nrm[j]
            v = v - mu[i, j] * Bs[j]
        Bs[i] = v; nrm[i] = v @ v
    k = 1
    while k < n:
        while valid <= k:
            gram_schmidt_row(valid); valid += 1
        for j in range(k - 1, -1, -1):                                  # size reduction
            q = int(round(mu[k, j]))
            if q:
                B[k] -= q * B[j]
                mu[k, :j + 1] -= q * np.concatenate((mu[j, :j], [1.0]))
        gram_schmidt_row(k)
        if nrm[k] >= (delta - mu[k, k - 1] ** 2) * nrm[k - 1]:        # Lovasz condition holds: move on
            k += 1
        else:                                                           # otherwise swap and step back
            B[[k, k - 1]] = B[[k - 1, k]]
            valid = max(k - 1, 0)
            k = max(k - 1, 1)
    return B.tolist()

def check_lll_reduced(basis, delta=0.98):
    # exact rational verification of the two LLL conditions (the float code above is not trusted)
    n = len(basis)
    Bs, mu = [], [[Fraction(0)] * n for _ in range(n)]
    sq = lambda v: sum(x * x for x in v)
    for i in range(n):
        v = [Fraction(x) for x in basis[i]]
        for j in range(i):
            mu[i][j] = sum(Fraction(a) * b for a, b in zip(basis[i], Bs[j])) / sq(Bs[j])
            v = [a - mu[i][j] * b for a, b in zip(v, Bs[j])]
        Bs.append(v)
    tol = Fraction(1, 10 ** 9)
    size_reduced = all(abs(mu[i][j]) <= Fraction(1, 2) + tol for i in range(n) for j in range(i))
    d = Fraction(delta).limit_denominator(1000)
    lovasz = all(sq(Bs[k]) >= (d - mu[k][k - 1] ** 2) * sq(Bs[k - 1]) - tol for k in range(1, n))
    return size_reduced, lovasz
rng = random.Random(2)
det2 = lambda M: M[0][0] * M[1][1] - M[0][1] * M[1][0]
norm = lambda v: math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in v))

# --- the same two-dimensional lattice described by a good basis and by a bad one
good = [[7, 2], [-3, 9]]
U = [[17, 10], [12, 7]]                                                # an integer matrix with determinant -1 (unimodular)
bad = [[sum(U[i][k] * good[k][j] for k in range(2)) for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)]
print("determinant of U:", det2(U), "| lattice volume from the good basis:", abs(det2(good)), "and from the bad basis:", abs(det2(bad)))
print("bad basis:", bad, "with lengths", [round(norm(v), 1) for v in bad])
reduced = lll(bad)
print("LLL on the bad basis:", reduced, "with lengths", [round(norm(v), 1) for v in reduced], "| good basis lengths", [round(norm(v), 1) for v in good])
print("LLL result verified exactly:", check_lll_reduced(reduced))

def hadamard_ratio(B):
    return (abs(round(np.linalg.det(np.array(B, dtype=float)))) / np.prod([norm(v) for v in B])) ** (1 / len(B))

# --- Babai's nearest-plane algorithm: decoding with a good basis works, with a bad basis it fails
n = 12
good = [[25 if i == j else rng.randint(-3, 3) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
M = [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
for _ in range(60):                                                    # a random unimodular matrix built from row operations
    i, j = rng.sample(range(n), 2)
    c = rng.choice((-2, -1, 1, 2))
    M[i] = [a + c * b for a, b in zip(M[i], M[j])]
bad = (np.array(M) @ np.array(good)).tolist()
reduced = lll(bad)
print("size of the largest entry: good basis", max(abs(x) for r in good for x in r), "| bad basis", max(abs(x) for r in bad for x in r), "| after LLL", max(abs(x) for r in reduced for x in r))
print("Hadamard ratio (1 = orthogonal): good %.2f, bad %.4f, LLL-reduced %.2f" % (hadamard_ratio(good), hadamard_ratio(bad), hadamard_ratio(reduced)))

def babai(B, target):
    Bf = np.array(B, dtype=float)
    Bs = np.zeros_like(Bf)
    for i in range(len(B)):
        Bs[i] = Bf[i] - sum((Bf[i] @ Bs[j]) / (Bs[j] @ Bs[j]) * Bs[j] for j in range(i))
    v = np.array(target, dtype=float)
    for i in reversed(range(len(B))):
        v = v - round((v @ Bs[i]) / (Bs[i] @ Bs[i])) * Bf[i]            # peel off one coordinate per Gram-Schmidt direction
    return np.array(target) - np.round(v)                                # the lattice point that was found

good_arr = np.array(good)
trials, wins = 300, {"good basis": 0, "bad basis": 0, "LLL-reduced bad basis": 0}
for _ in range(trials):
    coefficients = np.array([rng.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(n)])
    point = coefficients @ good_arr                                      # a random lattice point
    error = np.array([rng.randint(-6, 6) for _ in range(n)])
    target = point + error
    for name, basis in (("good basis", good), ("bad basis", bad), ("LLL-reduced bad basis", reduced)):
        wins[name] += bool(np.array_equal(babai(basis, target), point))
for name, count in wins.items():
    print(f"decoding a lattice point plus noise in [-6, 6]^12 with the {name}: {count} of {trials} correct")

blocks.markdown:
The determinant of the transformation is −1, so both bases describe the same lattice of volume 69, yet the bad basis has vectors of length 107 and 153 against 7 and 9 for the good one. LLL recovers exactly the good basis, and the exact rational check confirms both LLL conditions. In dimension 12 the effect on decoding is total: with the good basis Babai's algorithm recovers the right lattice point in all 300 trials, with the bad basis in **none**, and with the LLL-reduced version of the bad basis in all 300. The Hadamard ratio measures this orthogonality (1 for orthogonal vectors, 0.0136 for the bad basis).

This is the essence of the public/private key idea in lattice cryptography (the GGH-style intuition): publish a bad basis, keep a good one. It is also a warning: in *small* dimension LLL repairs a bad basis, so the dimension must be large enough that LLL and its stronger relatives fail. The next listing measures how far LLL gets from the best possible answer.

rng = random.Random(5)

def q_ary_kernel_basis(n, q, rng):
    # random lattice {x in Z^n : A x = 0 mod q} with n/2 constraints, as an explicit basis (volume q^(n/2))
    h = n // 2
    A1 = [[rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(h)] for _ in range(h)]
    basis = []
    for i in range(h):
        row = [0] * n; row[i] = 1
        for r in range(h): row[h + r] = (-A1[r][i]) % q
        basis.append(row)
    for r in range(h):
        row = [0] * n; row[h + r] = q; basis.append(row)
    return basis

def enumerate_shortest(B):
    # exact shortest vector by Fincke-Pohst enumeration over the coefficients of a reduced basis (small dimensions only)
    n = len(B)
    Bf = np.array(B, dtype=float)
    Bs = np.zeros_like(Bf); mu = np.zeros((n, n)); nrm = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n):
        Bs[i] = Bf[i]
        for j in range(i):
            mu[i, j] = Bf[i] @ Bs[j] / nrm[j]
            Bs[i] = Bs[i] - mu[i, j] * Bs[j]
        nrm[i] = Bs[i] @ Bs[i]
    best = [float(Bf[0] @ Bf[0]) - 1e-6, None]
    nodes = [0]
    def search(i, coefficients, partial):
        nodes[0] += 1
        centre = -sum(coefficients[j] * mu[j, i] for j in range(i + 1, n))
        radius = math.sqrt(max(best[0] - partial, 0) / nrm[i])
        for x in range(math.ceil(centre - radius), math.floor(centre + radius) + 1):
            coefficients[i] = x
            d = partial + (x - centre) ** 2 * nrm[i]
            if d > best[0]:
                continue
            if i == 0:
                if any(coefficients) and d < best[0]:
                    best[0], best[1] = d, list(coefficients)
            else:
                search(i - 1, coefficients, d)
        coefficients[i] = 0
    search(n - 1, [0] * n, 0.0)
    if best[1] is None:
        return B[0], nodes[0]
    return (np.array(best[1]) @ np.array(B)).tolist(), nodes[0]

blocks.markdown:
On random q-ary lattices the shortest vector LLL finds is within about 11 to 17 percent above the Gaussian-heuristic length for these dimensions, and the exact enumeration agrees with LLL in dimensions 8 to 16 (LLL happened to find a shortest vector each time here). The measured root Hermite factor per dimension, (|b1| / vol^(1/d))^(1/d), is between 0.99 and 1.015; these lattices contain the vector q·e_i, so for small dimensions |b1| is capped by q and the factor is smaller than for a generic lattice, and the figure should not be generalised. The guaranteed bound is much weaker than what LLL achieves. In high dimension this changes: the exponent in the guarantee, and the measured factor, make LLL useless against dimension-500 lattices, and the security analysis moves to BKZ, which calls an exact or sieving SVP solver on blocks of size β (B07, DeepBKZ chapter, section 2.2); lesson 8.10 turns that into numbers.

**Common mistakes:** treating the LLL guarantee as the real behaviour (it is a worst-case bound, practice is far better in small dimension), and treating small-dimension experiments as evidence about security (the toy results here say only that toy parameters are insecure).

sections.title: 8.2 LWE (Learning With Errors)
sections.summary: Regev-style encryption built and measured, why the error makes the problem hard, and a real lattice attack (Kannan embedding with LLL) that recovers secrets of toy size.

blocks.markdown:
The **Learning With Errors (LWE)** problem: a secret vector s in Z_q^n is fixed; each sample is a random vector a together with b = ⟨a, s⟩ + e (mod q), where e is a small error drawn from a narrow distribution. The **search** problem is to find s from many samples; the **decision** problem is to tell such samples from uniformly random ones. Without e this is linear algebra and Gaussian elimination solves it from n equations; with e it is believed hard, and Regev showed it is as hard as worst-case lattice problems (a result cited from the literature, not reproduced here). ML-KEM is built on a structured version of this problem (FIPS 203, section 3: "module-LWE"), and the ML-KEM secret and error use a centred binomial distribution (η in {2, 3}).

A **Regev-style public-key encryption** of one bit works as follows. The public key is (A, b = A s + e). To encrypt a bit, pick a random subset r of the rows, send c1 = rᵀA and c2 = rᵀb + bit·⌊q/2⌋. The receiver computes c2 − ⟨c1, s⟩ = ⟨r, e⟩ + bit·⌊q/2⌋ and decides by whether the result is near 0 or near q/2. It is correct as long as the accumulated noise ⟨r, e⟩ stays below q/4, and the first listing measures that margin, shows what happens when the error is too large, and contrasts the noise-free and the noisy problem. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

import math, random
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
q = 3329

def centered_binomial(eta, size):
    return rng.integers(0, 2, (*size, eta)).sum(-1) - rng.integers(0, 2, (*size, eta)).sum(-1)

# --- Regev-style public-key encryption of one bit from LWE
n, m, eta = 32, 128, 2
s = centered_binomial(eta, (n,))
A = rng.integers(0, q, (m, n))
e = centered_binomial(eta, (m,))
b = (A @ s + e) % q                                                     # the public key is (A, b): m noisy equations in the secret s

def encrypt(bit):
    r = rng.integers(0, 2, m)                                           # a random subset of the m equations
    return (r @ A) % q, (r @ b + bit * (q // 2)) % q

def decrypt(ciphertext):
    c1, c2 = ciphertext
    x = (c2 - c1 @ s) % q                                               # = r.e + bit * q/2 (mod q)
    return int(q // 4 < x < 3 * q // 4)

bits = rng.integers(0, 2, 2000)
print("decryption correct for", sum(decrypt(encrypt(int(t))) == t for t in bits), "of", len(bits), "random bits")
print("worst-case noise bound |r.e| <= m * max|e| =", m * 2, "against the decryption margin q/4 =", q // 4, "-> correct for every key and message")
sample = []
for _ in range(2000):
    r = rng.integers(0, 2, m)
    sample.append(int(r @ e))
print(f"measured noise r.e over 2000 encryptions: mean {np.mean(sample):.2f}, standard deviation {np.std(sample):.2f}, largest {max(abs(x) for x in sample)}; prediction |e| / 2 = {np.linalg.norm(e) / 2:.2f} for this particular error vector")

# --- too much noise breaks correctness: the same scheme with a larger error distribution
for width in (100, 200, 300, 400):
    e_big = rng.integers(-width, width + 1, m)
    b_big = (A @ s + e_big) % q
    fails = 0
    for t in bits[:1000]:
        r = rng.integers(0, 2, m)
        c1, c2 = (r @ A) % q, (r @ b_big + int(t) * (q // 2)) % q
        fails += int(q // 4 < (c2 - c1 @ s) % q < 3 * q // 4) != t
    print(f"error uniform in [-{width}, {width}]: {fails:>4} of 1000 decryptions wrong")

# --- without noise the problem is linear algebra: Gaussian elimination mod q recovers the secret from n equations
def solve_mod(A_rows, rhs, q):
    M = [list(map(int, row)) + [int(v)] for row, v in zip(A_rows, rhs)]
    size = len(M[0]) - 1
    for col in range(size):
        pivot = next(r for r in range(col, len(M)) if M[r][col] % q)
        M[col], M[pivot] = M[pivot], M[col]
        inv = pow(M[col][col], -1, q)
        M[col] = [x * inv % q for x in M[col]]
        for r in range(len(M)):
            if r != col and M[r][col]:
                factor = M[r][col]

With errors in [−2, 2] and 128 samples the worst possible noise is 256, far below q/4 = 832, so decryption is correct for every key and message (2,000 of 2,000 here), and the measured spread of the noise (6.11) matches the prediction |e|/2 = 6.12 for this key. When the error is widened the margin disappears: errors up to ±100 already give wrong decryptions for 18 of 1,000 bits, and at ±200 and ±300 the failure rate is 29 percent and 59 percent (it falls again at ±400 only because the noise wraps around modulo q). This is the **correctness/security tradeoff** of every LWE scheme: more noise is harder to attack but breaks decryption. Gaussian elimination recovers the secret from exact equations but returns a wrong answer on the noisy ones, which is the whole point of the error. The exhaustive-search demonstration in the last lines is feasible only because n = 4 and q = 17 (83,521 candidate secrets): it finds exactly one consistent secret for real samples and none for uniform samples, which is a **distinguisher**, and the search space for n = 256 and q = 3329 is 2^2995.

Brute force is not the real threat. The relevant attack turns LWE into a lattice problem: the vector (e, 1) is an unusually short vector in a lattice built from the public key. This is **Kannan's embedding** (B07, section 2.2), and the second listing mounts it with LLL against toy instances.

import math, random
import numpy as np
from fractions import Fraction

def lll(basis, delta=0.99):
    B = np.array(basis, dtype=np.int64)
    n = len(B)
    Bs = np.zeros((n, B.shape[1])); mu = np.zeros((n, n)); nrm = np.zeros(n)
    valid = 0
    def gram_schmidt_row(i):
        v = B[i].astype(float)
        for j in range(i):
            mu[i, j] = (B[i] @ Bs[j]) / nrm[j]
            v = v - mu[i, j] * Bs[j]
        Bs[i] = v; nrm[i] = v @ v
    k = 1
    while k < n:
        while valid <= k:
            gram_schmidt_row(valid); valid += 1
        for j in range(k - 1, -1, -1):                                  # size reduction
            q = int(round(mu[k, j]))
            if q:
                B[k] -= q * B[j]
                mu[k, :j + 1] -= q * np.concatenate((mu[j, :j], [1.0]))
        gram_schmidt_row(k)
        if nrm[k] >= (delta - mu[k, k - 1] ** 2) * nrm[k - 1]:        # Lovasz condition holds: move on
            k += 1
        else:                                                           # otherwise swap and step back
            B[[k, k - 1]] = B[[k - 1, k]]
            valid = max(k - 1, 0)
            k = max(k - 1, 1)
    return B.tolist()

def check_lll_reduced(basis, delta=0.98):
    # exact rational verification of the two LLL conditions (the float code above is not trusted)
    n = len(basis)
    Bs, mu = [], [[Fraction(0)] * n for _ in range(n)]
    sq = lambda v: sum(x * x for x in v)
    for i in range(n):
        v = [Fraction(x) for x in basis[i]]
        for j in range(i):
            mu[i][j] = sum(Fraction(a) * b for a, b in zip(basis[i], Bs[j])) / sq(Bs[j])
            v = [a - mu[i][j] * b for a, b in zip(v, Bs[j])]
        Bs.append(v)
    tol = Fraction(1, 10 ** 9)
    size_reduced = all(abs(mu[i][j]) <= Fraction(1, 2) + tol for i in range(n) for j in range(i))
    d = Fraction(delta).limit_denominator(1000)
    lovasz = all(sq(Bs[k]) >= (d - mu[k][k - 1] ** 2) * sq(Bs[k - 1]) - tol for k in range(1, n))
    return size_reduced, lovasz
rng = random.Random(3)

def lwe_instance(n, q, m, bound):
    # "normal form" LWE: A = [I | A'] makes the lattice basis explicit; b = s A + e with errors in [-bound, bound]
    A2 = [[rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(m - n)] for _ in range(n)]
    A = [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(n)] + A2[i] for i in range(n)]
    s = [rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(n)]
    e = [rng.randint(-bound, bound) for _ in range(m)]
    b = [(sum(s[i] * A[i][j] for i in range(n)) + e[j]) % q for j in range(m)]
    return A, s, e, b

def primal_attack(A, b, q, n, m, bound):
    # Kannan embedding: the lattice generated by the rows of A and q * I, plus the row (b, 1).
    # The vector (b, 1) minus the lattice point s*A is (e, 1), which is unusually short; LLL may expose it.
    basis = [row + [0] for row in A]
    for j in range(m - n):
        row = [0] * (m + 1); row[n + j] = q; basis.append(row)
    basis.append(list(b) + [1])
    reduced = lll(basis)
    for v in reduced:
        if abs(v[-1]) == 1:
            candidate = [x * v[-1] for x in v[:-1]]
            if max(abs(x) for x in candidate) <= bound:
                return candidate, reduced
    return None, reduced

q, bound = 97, 1
print(f"{'n':>3} {'samples m':>9} {'lattice dim':>12} {'error recovered':>16} {'secret recovered':>17}")
for n in (8, 16, 24, 32):
    m = 2 * n
    ok_e = ok_s = 0
    trials = 1 if n == 32 else 2
    for _ in range(trials):
        A, s, e, b = lwe_instance(n, q, m, bound)
        candidate, reduced = primal_attack(A, b, q, n, m, bound)
        if candidate == e:
            ok_e += 1
            recovered = [(b[i] - candidate[i]) % q for i in range(n)]       # the first n columns of A are the identity, so b - e starts with s
            ok_s += recovered == s
    print(f"{n:>3} {m:>9} {m + 1:>12} {ok_e:>13} / {trials} {ok_s:>14} / {trials}")

A, s, e, b = lwe_instance(8, q, 16, bound)
candidate, reduced = primal_attack(A, b, q, 8, 16, bound)
print("for n = 8 the LLL basis passes the exact check of both LLL conditions:", check_lll_reduced(reduced))
dim = 17
gaussian = math.sqrt(dim / (2 * math.pi * math.e)) * q ** ((16 - 8) / dim)
print(f"why the attack can work: |(e, 1)| = {math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in e) + 1):.2f}, while a typical shortest vector of a random lattice of this volume has length about {gaussian:.2f} (Gaussian heuristic), so (e, 1) is an unusually short, hence findable, vector")

LLL recovered the complete error vector, and hence the secret, in every trial for secret lengths 8, 16, 24 and 32 (with q = 97, errors in {−1, 0, 1} and twice as many samples as unknowns). The reason is geometric: the target vector (e, 1) has norm about 3.7 while a typical shortest vector of that lattice has length about 8.6, so it is the unique unusually short vector and the reduction exposes it. The same code with n = 40 and m = 80 failed in all three trials when I tried it during authoring (about 50 seconds each, not part of the listing); the point where plain LLL stops working is exactly why real parameters use n·k of 512 and more. Stronger reduction (BKZ with large blocks) moves that threshold, and lesson 8.10 estimates by how much.

**What this shows.** (1) The toy parameters are broken by a polynomial-time algorithm, so toy-size experiments can never support a security claim. (2) The attack needs the error to be *short*: the cost depends on the ratio between the error length and the lattice's natural scale, which is why the modulus q and the error width are chosen together. **Common mistake:** adding more samples always helps the attacker only up to a point; the estimator in 8.10 optimises the number of samples used.

sections.title: 8.3 Ring-LWE
sections.summary: Polynomial rings modulo x^256 + 1, the number-theoretic transform from FIPS 203 implemented and checked against schoolbook multiplication and kyber-py, and ring-LWE encryption with measured noise.

blocks.markdown:
Plain LWE needs a huge matrix. **Ring-LWE** replaces the integers by the ring R_q = Z_q[x]/(x^n + 1): an element is a polynomial of degree below n and multiplication wraps around with a sign change because x^n = −1 (a **negacyclic** convolution). One ring element then plays the role of a whole n × n matrix, so public keys shrink by a factor of n, and multiplication can be done with a fast transform. The price is extra structure that plain LWE does not have, and the security assumption is correspondingly stronger (ring-LWE).

The fast transform is the **number-theoretic transform (NTT)**, a Fourier transform over Z_q. For ML-KEM q = 3329 = 2^8 · 13 + 1 and n = 256 (FIPS 203, section 4.3), so q has a primitive 256th root of unity ζ = 17 but no 512th root: the transform splits x^256 + 1 only down to 128 factors of degree 2, and the final pointwise step multiplies degree-1 polynomials (the base-case multiplication of FIPS 203, Algorithms 11 and 12). The listing implements Algorithms 9 to 12 from the standard, checks the NTT product against schoolbook multiplication, counts the modular multiplications, and compares the transform with the one inside kyber-py. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

import random
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_512

q, n = 3329, 256
ZETA = 17                                                               # a primitive 256th root of unity modulo 3329 (FIPS 203, section 4.3)
bitrev7 = lambda i: int(format(i, "07b")[::-1], 2)
zetas = [pow(ZETA, bitrev7(i), q) for i in range(128)]
counter = {"mul": 0}
def mulq(a, b):
    counter["mul"] += 1
    return a * b % q

def ntt(f):                                                             # FIPS 203, Algorithm 9
    f = list(f); i = 1; length = 128
    while length >= 2:
        for start in range(0, 256, 2 * length):
            zeta = zetas[i]; i += 1
            for j in range(start, start + length):
                t = mulq(zeta, f[j + length])
                f[j + length] = (f[j] - t) % q
                f[j] = (f[j] + t) % q
        length //= 2
    return f

def inverse_ntt(f):                                                     # FIPS 203, Algorithm 10
    f = list(f); i = 127; length = 2
    while length <= 128:
        for start in range(0, 256, 2 * length):
            zeta = zetas[i]; i -= 1
            for j in range(start, start + length):
                t = f[j]
                f[j] = (t + f[j + length]) % q
                f[j + length] = mulq(zeta, (f[j + length] - t) % q)
        length *= 2
    return [mulq(x, 3303) for x in f]                                   # 3303 = 128^-1 mod 3329

def multiply_ntts(f, g):                                                # FIPS 203, Algorithms 11 and 12: 128 products of degree-1 polynomials
    h = [0] * 256
    for i in range(128):
        gamma = pow(ZETA, 2 * bitrev7(i) + 1, q)
        a0, a1, b0, b1 = f[2 * i], f[2 * i + 1], g[2 * i], g[2 * i + 1]
        h[2 * i] = (mulq(a0, b0) + mulq(mulq(a1, b1), gamma)) % q
        h[2 * i + 1] = (mulq(a0, b1) + mulq(a1, b0)) % q
    return h

def schoolbook(f, g):                                                   # multiplication in Z_q[x] / (x^256 + 1): x^256 = -1
    h = [0] * 256
    for i in range(256):
        for j in range(256):
            k = i + j
            if k < 256: h[k] = (h[k] + f[i] * g[j]) % q
            else: h[k - 256] = (h[k - 256] - f[i] * g[j]) % q
    return h

rng = random.Random(9)
print("q - 1 =", q - 1, "= 2^8 * 13, so q has 256th roots of unity but no 512th root:", pow(ZETA, 128, q) == q - 1, "(zeta^128 = -1)", "| (q - 1) divisible by 512:", (q - 1) % 512 == 0)
f = [rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(256)]
g = [rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(256)]
print("inverse NTT undoes the NTT:", inverse_ntt(ntt(f)) == f)
counter["mul"] = 0
product_ntt = inverse_ntt(multiply_ntts(ntt(f), ntt(g)))
ntt_cost = counter["mul"]
print("NTT-based product equals the schoolbook product mod x^256 + 1:", product_ntt == schoolbook(f, g), "| 20 more random pairs:", all(
    inverse_ntt(multiply_ntts(ntt(a), ntt(b))) == schoolbook(a, b) for a, b in ((([rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(256)]), ([rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(256)])) for _ in range(20))))
print(f"modular multiplications: schoolbook {256 * 256:,}; NTT route {ntt_cost:,} (two forward NTTs, 128 base-case products, one inverse NTT), about {256 * 256 / ntt_cost:.0f} times fewer")

reference = ML_KEM_512.R(list(f)).to_ntt().coeffs                  # kyber-py transforms the list in place, so pass a copy
print("my NTT of f equals the NTT inside kyber-py:", list(reference) == ntt(f))
unit = [0] * 256; unit[1] = 1
xpow = f
for _ in range(256):                                                    # multiplying by x 256 times is multiplying by x^256 = -1
    xpow = schoolbook(xpow, unit)
print("negacyclic wrap: x^256 times f equals -f:", xpow == [(-c) % q for c in f])
print("the NTT is a ring isomorphism: product of NTTs is the NTT of the product (coefficient-wise on 128 degree-1 pieces):", multiply_ntts(ntt(f), ntt(g)) == ntt(schoolbook(f, g)))

import math
import numpy as np

q, n, eta = 3329, 256, 2
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

def cbd(size=n):
    return rng.integers(0, 2, (size, eta)).sum(1) - rng.integers(0, 2, (size, eta)).sum(1)

def ring_mul(f, g):
    # product in Z_q[x] / (x^256 + 1): the part of the product above degree 255 wraps around with a minus sign
    c = np.convolve(f, g)
    c = np.concatenate((c, np.zeros(2 * n - len(c), dtype=c.dtype)))
    return (c[:n] - c[n:]) % q

# --- ring-LWE public-key encryption of 256 bits at once (message bit i is carried by coefficient i)
a = rng.integers(0, q, n)                                              # one uniformly random ring element is the whole "matrix"
s, e = cbd(), cbd()
b = (ring_mul(a, s) + e) % q
half = (q + 1) // 2                                                    # 1665, the encoding of a 1 bit

def encrypt(message):
    r, e1, e2 = cbd(), cbd(), cbd()
    u = (ring_mul(a, r) + e1) % q
    v = (ring_mul(b, r) + e2 + half * message) % q
    return u, v

def decrypt(u, v):
    x = (v - ring_mul(s, u)) % q
    return ((x > q // 4) & (x < 3 * q // 4)).astype(int)

trials, wrong_bits, noise_samples = 300, 0, []
for _ in range(trials):
    message = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
    u, v = encrypt(message)
    wrong_bits += int((decrypt(u, v) != message).sum())
    noise = ((v - ring_mul(s, u) - half * message + q // 2) % q) - q // 2          # the decryption noise, centred around 0
    noise_samples.append(noise)
noise_samples = np.concatenate(noise_samples)
print(f"{trials} encryptions of 256 random bits: {wrong_bits} wrong bits out of {trials * n:,}")
variance = 2 * n * 1.0 * 1.0 + 1.0                                     # Var(e r) + Var(s e1) + Var(e2), each coefficient with variance eta/2 = 1
print(f"decryption noise: standard deviation {noise_samples.std():.2f} measured, {math.sqrt(variance):.2f} predicted (sqrt(2 * 256 + 1)); largest seen {int(np.abs(noise_samples).max())}")
print(f"the failure threshold q/4 = {q // 4} is {(q // 4) / math.sqrt(variance):.0f} standard deviations away, so failures never occur in practice")

# --- what the ring structure buys: size of the public matrix
unstructured_bits = n * n * 12                                         # a 256 x 256 matrix of 12-bit numbers (LWE with the same secret length)
ring_bits = n * 12                                                     # one ring element describes the whole matrix
print(f"public matrix for secret length 256: unstructured LWE {unstructured_bits // 8:,} bytes, ring-LWE {ring_bits // 8:,} bytes (factor {unstructured_bits // ring_bits})")
rows = np.array([np.roll(a, i) for i in range(n)])                      # multiplication by a is a 256 x 256 matrix that is determined by its first row
for i in range(n):
    rows[i, :i] = (-rows[i, :i]) % q                                    # entries that wrapped around pick up a minus sign
x = rng.integers(0, q, n)
print("multiplying by a equals multiplying by a negacyclic 256 x 256 matrix built from a single row:", np.array_equal((x @ rows) % q, ring_mul(a, x)))
print("so a ring-LWE sample is an LWE sample whose matrix has this special structure; the extra structure is the extra assumption")

All 76,800 encrypted bits decrypt correctly. The decryption noise has measured standard deviation 23.2 against the predicted sqrt(2·256 + 1) = 22.65 (each coefficient of e·r and s·e1 is a sum of 256 products of unit-variance values, plus e2), so the failure threshold q/4 = 832 is about 37 standard deviations away. The ring structure shrinks the public matrix for a secret of length 256 from 98,304 bytes to 384 bytes, a factor of 256, and the last check shows that multiplication by one polynomial *is* multiplication by a 256 × 256 matrix that is fixed by its first row (with sign changes for the wrapped entries). A ring-LWE sample is therefore an LWE sample with a structured matrix, and every attack on plain LWE applies, while a hypothetical attack could also exploit the structure; no such attack better than the general ones is known for these parameters, and that is an assumption and not a theorem.

**Common mistakes:** forgetting the sign when a product wraps past x^255 (this gives a cyclic and not a negacyclic ring, with different security properties), and confusing the NTT-domain representation with coefficients when serialising (FIPS 203 keeps keys in a defined byte format for exactly this reason).

sections.title: 8.4 Module-LWE
sections.summary: A module-LWE sample seen as a structured integer LWE sample, and the ML-KEM sizes and parameters reproduced from FIPS 203 and checked against kyber-py.

blocks.markdown:
**Module-LWE** sits between the two extremes. The public matrix A is a k × k matrix of ring elements, and the secret and error are vectors of k ring elements. With k = 1 it is ring-LWE; with n = 1 and large k it is plain LWE. A module scheme reaches different security levels by changing the **rank k** while the ring, the modulus and the noise stay the same, which is why ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024 differ mainly in k = 2, 3, 4 (FIPS 203, Table 2) and why the same optimised ring arithmetic serves all three. A smaller structure than ring-LWE per level, a larger one than plain LWE, makes the extra-structure assumption weaker than for ring-LWE of the same dimension.

The first listing computes a module-LWE sample with ring arithmetic and again as an ordinary integer LWE sample with a 512 × 512 matrix built from negacyclic blocks, and shows that the two views agree. The second reproduces the key and ciphertext size formulas of ML-KEM from the parameters and compares them with FIPS 203 Table 3 and with the real objects produced by kyber-py. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

import numpy as np

q, n, eta = 3329, 256, 2
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
cbd = lambda: rng.integers(0, 2, (n, eta)).sum(1) - rng.integers(0, 2, (n, eta)).sum(1)

def ring_mul(f, g):
    c = np.convolve(f, g)
    c = np.concatenate((c, np.zeros(2 * n - len(c), dtype=c.dtype)))
    return (c[:n] - c[n:]) % q

def negacyclic_block(a):
    # the n x n integer matrix M(a) with M(a) @ x = a * x in the ring (column j holds a * x^j)
    M = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=np.int64)
    for j in range(n):
        shifted = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int64)
        shifted[j:] = a[:n - j]
        shifted[:j] = -a[n - j:]                                        # coefficients that pass x^255 come back negated
        M[:, j] = shifted % q
    return M

k = 2                                                                   # module rank of ML-KEM-512
A = [[rng.integers(0, q, n) for _ in range(k)] for _ in range(k)]       # a k x k matrix of ring elements
s = [cbd() for _ in range(k)]
e = [cbd() for _ in range(k)]

# the module-LWE sample b = A s + e, computed with ring arithmetic
b_ring = [(sum(ring_mul(A[i][j], s[j]) for j in range(k)) + e[i]) % q for i in range(k)]

# the same sample as an ordinary LWE sample: a (k*n) x (k*n) integer matrix, secret and error of length k*n
big = np.block([[negacyclic_block(A[i][j]) for j in range(k)] for i in range(k)])
b_flat = (big @ np.concatenate(s) + np.concatenate(e)) % q
print("module-LWE sample, ring view and integer-matrix view agree:", np.array_equal(np.concatenate(b_ring), b_flat))
print(f"the equivalent LWE problem has dimension {k * n} (secret length), an integer matrix with {big.size:,} entries, but only {k * k * n:,} of them are independent")
print("independent entries / matrix entries =", f"1/{big.size // (k * k * n)}", "- this redundancy is the algebraic structure that standard LWE does not have")

print()
print("the module rank k sets the secret length n * k (n = 256) and the size of the public matrix:")
print(f"{'k':>3} {'secret length':>14} {'ring elements in A':>19} {'size of A (12-bit coefficients)':>32} {'unstructured LWE, same secret length':>38}")
for kk in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    print(f"{kk:>3} {kk * n:>14} {kk * kk:>19} {kk * kk * n * 12 // 8:>26,} bytes {(kk * n) ** 2 * 12 // 8:>32,} bytes")

sections.title: 8.5 SIS/Module-SIS
sections.summary: The short integer solution problem as a hash-collision problem, an LLL attack that finds a collision for the smallest toy and fails for larger ones, and the ring structure of ML-DSA.

blocks.markdown:
The **Short Integer Solution (SIS)** problem: given a random matrix A in Z_q^(n×m), find a non-zero short integer vector x with A x = 0 (mod q). It is the dual partner of LWE and the basis of lattice signatures and hashing. **Ajtai's hash** h(x) = A x mod q on bit strings x in {0,1}^m compresses when m > n log2 q, and a collision (x1 ≠ x2 with h(x1) = h(x2)) is exactly a SIS solution x1 − x2 with entries in {−1, 0, 1}, so finding collisions is as hard as SIS. The vectors with A x = 0 form a q-ary lattice of volume q^n, so SIS is a short-vector problem in that lattice, and LLL applies. **Module-SIS** replaces integers by module elements over R_q in the same way module-LWE does.

ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is a lattice signature built on these problems; the design reduces forgery to module-SIS and key recovery to module-LWE (a statement from the design literature, not from the standard text). The first listing builds Ajtai hashes of increasing size and attacks them with LLL; the second reproduces the ML-DSA parameters and key and signature sizes from FIPS 204 and checks them against dilithium-py. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

import math, random
import numpy as np
from fractions import Fraction

def lll(basis, delta=0.99):
    B = np.array(basis, dtype=np.int64)
    n = len(B)
    Bs = np.zeros((n, B.shape[1])); mu = np.zeros((n, n)); nrm = np.zeros(n)
    valid = 0
    def gram_schmidt_row(i):
        v = B[i].astype(float)
        for j in range(i):
            mu[i, j] = (B[i] @ Bs[j]) / nrm[j]
            v = v - mu[i, j] * Bs[j]
        Bs[i] = v; nrm[i] = v @ v
    k = 1
    while k < n:
        while valid <= k:
            gram_schmidt_row(valid); valid += 1
        for j in range(k - 1, -1, -1):                                  # size reduction
            q = int(round(mu[k, j]))
            if q:
                B[k] -= q * B[j]
                mu[k, :j + 1] -= q * np.concatenate((mu[j, :j], [1.0]))
        gram_schmidt_row(k)
        if nrm[k] >= (delta - mu[k, k - 1] ** 2) * nrm[k - 1]:        # Lovasz condition holds: move on
            k += 1
        else:                                                           # otherwise swap and step back
            B[[k, k - 1]] = B[[k - 1, k]]
            valid = max(k - 1, 0)
            k = max(k - 1, 1)
    return B.tolist()

def check_lll_reduced(basis, delta=0.98):
    # exact rational verification of the two LLL conditions (the float code above is not trusted)
    n = len(basis)
    Bs, mu = [], [[Fraction(0)] * n for _ in range(n)]
    sq = lambda v: sum(x * x for x in v)
    for i in range(n):
        v = [Fraction(x) for x in basis[i]]
        for j in range(i):
            mu[i][j] = sum(Fraction(a) * b for a, b in zip(basis[i], Bs[j])) / sq(Bs[j])
            v = [a - mu[i][j] * b for a, b in zip(v, Bs[j])]
        Bs.append(v)
    tol = Fraction(1, 10 ** 9)
    size_reduced = all(abs(mu[i][j]) <= Fraction(1, 2) + tol for i in range(n) for j in range(i))
    d = Fraction(delta).limit_denominator(1000)
    lovasz = all(sq(Bs[k]) >= (d - mu[k][k - 1] ** 2) * sq(Bs[k - 1]) - tol for k in range(1, n))
    return size_reduced, lovasz
rng = random.Random(1)

def sis_instance(n, q, m):
    # A = [A' | I] (n x m) over Z_q. The lattice {x : A x = 0 mod q} has an explicit basis and volume q^n.
    A1 = [[rng.randrange(q) for _ in range(m - n)] for _ in range(n)]
    A = [row + [1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(n)] for i, row in enumerate(A1)]
    basis = []
    for i in range(m - n):
        row = [0] * m; row[i] = 1
        for r in range(n): row[m - n + r] = (-A1[r][i]) % q
        basis.append(row)
    for r in range(n):
        row = [0] * m; row[m - n + r] = q; basis.append(row)
    return A, basis

def matvec(A, x, q):
    return [sum(a * b for a, b in zip(row, x)) % q for row in A]

q = 257
print("Ajtai-style hash h(x) = A x mod q on bit strings x in {0,1}^m; a collision is two different bit strings with the same hash")
print(f"{'n':>3} {'m':>4} {'input bits':>10} {'output bits':>12} {'shortest LLL vector':>20} {'largest entry':>14} {'collision?'}")
for n, m in ((6, 60), (8, 80), (10, 100), (12, 120)):
    A, basis = sis_instance(n, q, m)
    reduced = lll(basis)
    v = min(reduced, key=lambda x: sum(a * a for a in x))
    norm = math.sqrt(sum(a * a for a in v))
    largest = max(abs(a) for a in v)
    verdict = ""
    if largest <= 1:
        x1 = [1 if a == 1 else 0 for a in v]                           # the positive part of the short vector
        x2 = [1 if a == -1 else 0 for a in v]                          # the negative part: A (x1 - x2) = 0, so A x1 = A x2
        assert x1 != x2 and matvec(A, x1, q) == matvec(A, x2, q)
        verdict = f"yes: two distinct inputs with {sum(x1)} and {sum(x2)} ones hash to the same value"
    else:
        verdict = f"no: an entry of size {largest} is not a difference of two bit strings"
    print(f"{n:>3} {m:>4} {m:>10} {round(n * math.log2(q)):>12} {norm:>20.2f} {largest:>14} {verdict}")

print()
print("the pigeonhole bound says collisions exist once 2^m > q^n; the attack needs more: a short enough kernel vector")
for n, m in ((6, 60), (8, 80), (10, 100), (12, 120)):
    ternary_vectors = math.log2(3) * m - n * math.log2(q)
    print(f"n = {n:>2}, m = {m:>2}: expected number of kernel vectors with entries in {{-1, 0, 1}} is about 2^{ternary_vectors:.0f}" if ternary_vectors > 0 else f"n = {n:>2}, m = {m:>2}: no ternary kernel vector is expected")

For the smallest instance (n = 6, m = 60, so 60 input bits against 48 output bits) LLL finds a kernel vector with entries in {−1, 0, 1}; splitting it into its positive and negative parts gives two different bit strings that hash to the same value, a **real collision** verified by the code. For the larger instances LLL finds shorter vectors (norm 5 to 9) but their largest entry is 2, so they are **not** differences of bit strings: no collision. The last lines explain why this is a limit of the algorithm and not of the problem: for n = 8, m = 80 about 2^63 ternary kernel vectors are expected to exist, but LLL does not find one. That is the gap between *existence* and *findability* on which SIS-based security rests, and it widens quickly with dimension.

Now the real parameters.

The ML-DSA parameter sets in dilithium-py equal FIPS 204 Table 1, β = τ·η holds for all three, and the key and signature size formulas reproduce Table 2 (1,312, 2,560 and 2,420 bytes for ML-DSA-44, and the corresponding values for -65 and -87) and the sizes of real keys and signatures. The matrix A of ML-DSA-44 is 4 × 4 over R_q, giving a module-SIS instance with 2,048 unknowns and 1,024 equations.

**Why SIS and LWE appear together.** An LWE-based public key hides a secret in noisy equations, and a SIS-based signature proves knowledge of a short solution without revealing it; both are short-vector problems in lattices of related shape, which is why one estimator (8.10) covers both. **Common mistake:** equating "LLL did not find a collision" with "no collision exists" — the toy shows that collisions exist in abundance and only the search is hard.

sections.title: 8.6 Merkle Trees
sections.summary: Authentication paths reproduced from the slides (nodes 26, 13, 6, 3, 1 and siblings 27, 12, 7, 2), tamper detection, path sizes, and a leaf/inner-node confusion that domain separation prevents.

blocks.markdown:
A **Merkle tree** authenticates many values with one short public value. For 2^d keys K1, ..., K(2^d) the leaves are the hashes of the keys, every inner node is the hash of its two children's concatenation, and the **root** is the public key. To prove that K_i belongs to the tree, a signer supplies K_i and the **sibling nodes along the path** from its leaf to the root, d hash values in all; the verifier recomputes the root and compares (B03, Stinson, the slides on Merkle trees). In the numbering of the slides node j has children 2j and 2j + 1, leaf K_i is node i + 2^d − 1, and the sibling of node j is j + 1 if j is even and j − 1 if odd. The tree is only used to authenticate the public keys of **one-time** signatures, which sign the actual messages; this is how a hash-based scheme turns one-time keys into 2^d signatures with a single public key (the idea of 1979 that XMSS and SLH-DSA build on).

The listing reproduces the slides' depth-4 example (signing message 11 uses nodes 26, 13, 6, 3, 1 and supplies 27, 12, 7, 2), authenticates all 16 keys, tests modified keys and wrong positions, and shows how the path length grows with the height. It then demonstrates a subtle flaw of the plain definition V(j) = h(V(2j) ‖ V(2j+1)): an inner node's two children, concatenated, look exactly like a 64-byte leaf, so without **domain separation** a verifier that does not insist on fixed-length keys can be fooled. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, random

H = lambda data: hashlib.sha256(data).digest()
rng = random.Random(6)

# --- the depth-4 tree of the slides: leaf keys K1..K16 sit at nodes 16..31, node j has children 2j and 2j+1
def build_tree(keys, leaf_hash, node_hash):
    d = len(keys).bit_length() - 1
    assert len(keys) == 2 ** d
    V = {}
    for i, key in enumerate(keys):
        V[2 ** d + i] = leaf_hash(key)
    for j in range(2 ** d - 1, 0, -1):
        V[j] = node_hash(V[2 * j], V[2 * j + 1])
    return V, d

def auth_path(d, i):
    # for key K_i (i = 1..2^d) return the nodes on the path to the root and the sibling nodes that must be supplied
    node = i + 2 ** d - 1
    path, siblings = [node], []
    while node > 1:
        siblings.append(node + 1 if node % 2 == 0 else node - 1)
        node //= 2
        path.append(node)
    return path, siblings

def verify(key, i, supplied, d, root, leaf_hash, node_hash):
    node, value = i + 2 ** d - 1, leaf_hash(key)
    for sibling_value in supplied:
        value = node_hash(value, sibling_value) if node % 2 == 0 else node_hash(sibling_value, value)
        node //= 2
    return value == root

naive_leaf, naive_node = (lambda k: H(k)), (lambda l, r: H(l + r))                           # the slides' definition: V(j) = h(V(2j) || V(2j+1))
safe_leaf, safe_node = (lambda k: H(b"\x00" + k)), (lambda l, r: H(b"\x01" + l + r))         # domain separation between leaves and inner nodes

keys = [bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(32)) for _ in range(16)]                     # stand-ins for one-time public keys K1..K16
V, d = build_tree(keys, naive_leaf, naive_node)
path, siblings = auth_path(d, 11)
print("signing message 11: nodes on the path", path, "| sibling nodes to supply", siblings, "(the slides give 26, 13, 6, 3, 1 and 27, 12, 7, 2)")
supplied = [V[j] for j in siblings]
print("authentication of K11 against the root:", verify(keys[10], 11, supplied, d, V[1], naive_leaf, naive_node), "| signature carries", len(supplied), "hash values =", 32 * len(supplied), "bytes of path")
print("all 16 keys authenticate:", all(verify(keys[i - 1], i, [V[j] for j in auth_path(d, i)[1]], d, V[1], naive_leaf, naive_node) for i in range(1, 17)))
print("a modified key is rejected:", not verify(keys[10][:-1] + b"X", 11, supplied, d, V[1], naive_leaf, naive_node), "| the right key at the wrong position is rejected:", not verify(keys[10], 12, supplied, d, V[1], naive_leaf, naive_node))

print()
print("size against tree height (one hash value of 32 bytes per level):", {height: 32 * height for height in (4, 10, 16, 20)}, "bytes of authentication path; the public key stays one 32-byte root")

# --- second-preimage confusion between a leaf and an inner node when hashes are not domain separated
V4, d4 = build_tree(keys[:4], naive_leaf, naive_node)                                        # an honest 4-leaf tree and its root
root_honest = V4[1]
fake_leaf_data = V4[2] + V4[3]                                                               # the two level-1 hashes, 64 bytes, presented as ONE leaf "key"
print("without domain separation, a single fake 64-byte leaf hashes to the honest root:", naive_leaf(fake_leaf_data) == root_honest)
V4s, _ = build_tree(keys[:4], safe_leaf, safe_node)
fake_root_safe = safe_leaf(V4s[2] + V4s[3])
print("with a 0x00 prefix for leaves and 0x01 for inner nodes, the same trick gives a different value:", fake_root_safe != V4s[1])
print("a verifier that accepts a path of length 0 for the fake leaf would accept a 64-byte 'public key' for the honest tree in the naive scheme:", verify(fake_leaf_data, 1, [], 0, root_honest, naive_leaf, naive_node), "| in the separated scheme:", verify(fake_leaf_data, 1, [], 0, V4s[1], safe_leaf, safe_node))

blocks.markdown:
The code derives exactly the path and sibling nodes of the slides, and all 16 keys authenticate, while a modified key or the right key at the wrong position is rejected. A path is only d·32 bytes: 640 bytes for a tree with 2^20 leaves, while the public key stays 32 bytes. The last three lines show the confusion attack concretely: the concatenation of two level-1 hashes, presented as one 64-byte leaf, hashes to the honest root in the naive scheme, and a verifier that accepts a zero-length path would accept it; with a 0x00 prefix for leaves and a 0x01 prefix for inner nodes the values differ and the same trick fails. In a one-time-signature setting the keys have a fixed length, which also blocks the trick, but domain separation is a cheap, robust defence and is standard practice (for example the certificate-transparency Merkle tree construction does this); SLH-DSA instead uses addresses that identify every hash call by its position and type.

**Common mistakes:** accepting variable-length leaves, omitting the position (the index) from verification so that a valid key can be claimed at another position, and forgetting that the scheme's security also depends on the one-time signature never signing twice (8.7).

sections.title: 8.7 Hash-Based Signatures
sections.summary: Lamport and Winternitz signatures reproduced from the slides, key reuse and checksum attacks run exhaustively, HORS reuse, and the SLH-DSA size formulas checked against FIPS 205.

blocks.markdown:
**Hash-based signatures** need only a secure hash function, which is why their security is the best understood of the post-quantum families (B03). **Lamport's one-time scheme** (1979) signs a k-bit message by choosing, for each bit position i, two secret values y(i,0) and y(i,1) and publishing their images z(i,j) = f(y(i,j)); the signature reveals y(i, x_i) for each message bit x_i, and the verifier checks f(y(i,x_i)) = z(i,x_i). Each key signs **once**. The **Winternitz** scheme shortens signatures with hash chains: a w-bit digit x is signed by revealing the x-th element of a chain of 2^w − 1 hash applications, and the verifier hashes the remaining 2^w − 1 − x steps to reach the public end of the chain. Because anyone can hash *forward*, a **checksum** C = Σ(2^w − 1 − x_i) is signed as well, so raising one digit forces another to drop, which would need hashing *backward*. **HORS** is a few-time scheme: the message hash selects a k-subset of t secret values to reveal, and security degrades as the revealed subsets cover more of the keys. The standard **SLH-DSA** (FIPS 205) combines WOTS+ one-time keys, XMSS-style trees (8.6), a hypertree of d layers and FORS few-time signatures at the leaves.

The first listing reproduces the slides' toy Lamport example with f(y) = 3^y mod 7879 (and shows that a function with an easy inverse gives no security), and then implements Lamport with SHA-256 and measures what **key reuse** costs. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

Because 3^y mod 7879 can be inverted by brute force, the forged signature on (0, 1, 1) verifies: **a one-time signature is only as secure as its one-way function**. After six signatures the attacker needed only 10 hash evaluations to find a new message whose digest bits are all already revealed, and the forged signature was accepted by the real verifier. That is why a one-time key **must never sign twice**, and why stateful schemes treat state reuse as a catastrophic failure (a backup restored twice can reuse a key).

Next the Winternitz example of the slides, with an exhaustive check of the checksum, and the HORS attack.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, itertools, math, random

# --- Winternitz one-time signatures with w = 3 bits per chain, as in the slides (k = 9 message bits, 3 chains)
H = lambda data: hashlib.sha256(data).digest()
W, TOP = 3, 2 ** 3 - 1                                                  # chain length 2^w - 1 = 7 applications of the hash
def chain(value, steps):
    for _ in range(steps):
        value = H(value)
    return value
def chunks(bits9):
    return [int(bits9[i:i + 3], 2) for i in range(0, 9, 3)]
def checksum_chunks(xs):
    c = sum(TOP - x for x in xs)                                          # C = sum (2^w - 1 - x_i)
    return c, [int(format(c, "06b")[i:i + 3], 2) for i in (0, 3)]        # C padded to 6 bits, split into two 3-bit chunks

rng = random.Random(4)
secret = [bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(32)) for _ in range(5)]         # three message chains and two checksum chains
public = [chain(s, TOP) for s in secret]

def sign(bits9, with_checksum=True):
    xs = chunks(bits9)
    if with_checksum:
        xs = xs + checksum_chunks(xs[:3])[1]
    return [chain(secret[i], x) for i, x in enumerate(xs)], xs
def verify(sig, xs):
    return all(chain(a, TOP - x) == public[i] for i, (a, x) in enumerate(zip(sig, xs)))

message = "011101001"
xs = chunks(message)
C, extra = checksum_chunks(xs)
print("message 011101001 gives chunks", xs, "| checksum C =", C, "= binary", format(C, "04b"), "-> chunks", extra, "(slides: 3, 5, 1; C = 12 = 1100; chunks 1 and 4)")
signature, all_chunks = sign(message)
print("signature verifies:", verify(signature, all_chunks), f"| size {len(signature)} hash values for a {len(message)}-bit message")

# --- without the checksum the scheme is forgeable: hashing a revealed chain value forward gives any larger chunk
simple_signature, simple_chunks = sign(message, with_checksum=False)
forged_message = "101110100"
forged_chunks = chunks(forged_message)
forged = [chain(simple_signature[i], forged_chunks[i] - simple_chunks[i]) for i in range(3)]
print("without checksum, a forged signature on 101110100 built only by hashing forward (x' = 5, 6, 4 are each at least x = 3, 5, 1):", all(chain(a, TOP - x) == public[i] for i, (a, x) in enumerate(zip(forged, forged_chunks))))
forgeable_without = sum(1 for m in range(512) if all(a >= b for a, b in zip(chunks(format(m, "09b")), xs))) - 1
print("number of other messages forgeable that way without a checksum:", forgeable_without, "(= (8-3)(8-5)(8-1) - 1)")

# --- with the checksum: exhaustive check over all 512 messages
def attacker_can_derive(target_message):
    t = chunks(target_message); t = t + checksum_chunks(t)[1]
    return all(a >= b for a, b in zip(t, all_chunks))                     # a chain can only be advanced, never moved back
forgeable_with = [format(m, "09b") for m in range(512) if format(m, "09b") != message and attacker_can_derive(format(m, "09b"))]
print("with the checksum, messages whose signature can be derived from this one by hashing forward:", len(forgeable_with), "of 511 -> raising a message chunk lowers the checksum, which would need a chain value to be moved backwards")

# --- HORS few-time signatures: the attack from the slides (t = 32 keys, k = 4 revealed per signature)
sets = [{13, 21, 25, 27}, {5, 6, 13, 24}, {2, 21, 26, 30}, {5, 8, 18, 27}, {4, 9, 26, 29}]
target = {2, 13, 18, 29}
union = set().union(*sets)
print("indices revealed by the five signatures:", sorted(union), "| the sixth message needs", sorted(target), "-> all already revealed:", target <= union)
rng = random.Random(10)
t_keys, k_rev, trials = 32, 4, 20000
print(f"one signature reveals 4 of 32 keys; a random new message needs a specific 4-subset, chance 1 / C(32, 4) = 1 / {math.comb(t_keys, k_rev):,}")
print(f"{'signatures seen':>16} {'average keys revealed':>22} {'chance that a random new message can be forged (simulation, 20,000 trials)':>74}")
for seen in (2, 4, 8, 12, 16):
    forged_count, revealed_total = 0, 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        known = set()
        for _ in range(seen):
            known |= set(rng.sample(range(32), k_rev))
        revealed_total += len(known)
        forged_count += set(rng.sample(range(32), k_rev)) <= known
    print(f"{seen:>16} {revealed_total / trials:>22.1f} {forged_count / trials:>74.4f}")

sections.title: 8.8 Coding Theory
sections.summary: Hamming and Golay codes built and checked exhaustively: parity checks, syndromes, weight distributions, perfect codes, and the Gilbert-Varshamov guarantee.

blocks.markdown:
A **binary linear code** [n, k, d] is a k-dimensional subspace of GF(2)^n; its words are the **codewords**, and d is the **minimum distance** (smallest weight of a non-zero codeword), so the code corrects any ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors. A code can be described by a **parity-check matrix** H: a word c is a codeword when H c = 0, and for a received word r = c + e the **syndrome** H r = H e depends only on the error. If all error patterns of weight up to t have distinct syndromes, a table maps each syndrome to its error and decoding is a lookup. A code is **perfect** when the spheres of radius t around the codewords tile the whole space exactly; the Hamming codes (t = 1) and the binary **Golay code** [23, 12, 7] (t = 3) are the classical perfect codes. The **Gilbert-Varshamov** bound guarantees that good codes exist; it is non-constructive, and good *random* codes have no known efficient decoder, which is the foundation of code-based cryptography (8.9).

The listing builds the Hamming [7, 4] code and the Golay [23, 12] code (as a cyclic code with generator polynomial x^11 + x^10 + x^6 + x^5 + x^4 + x^2 + 1) and verifies every property above by exhaustive enumeration. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

import itertools, math, random
from collections import Counter

rng = random.Random(12)
weight = lambda x: bin(x).count("1")

# --- Hamming [7, 4, 3]: the syndrome of a single error is the binary number of its position
H = [[(col >> row) & 1 for col in range(1, 8)] for row in range(3)]      # parity-check matrix: column j is the binary representation of j
def syndrome_hamming(word_bits):
    return sum((sum(H[r][c] * word_bits[c] for c in range(7)) % 2) << r for r in range(3))
codewords = [w for w in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=7) if syndrome_hamming(w) == 0]
print("Hamming code: number of codewords", len(codewords), "= 2^4 | minimum distance", min(sum(w) for w in codewords if any(w)))
fixed = 0
for word in codewords:
    for pos in range(7):
        received = list(word); received[pos] ^= 1
        s = syndrome_hamming(received)
        received[s - 1] ^= 1                                              # the syndrome names the flipped position (1-based)
        fixed += tuple(received) == word
print("every single-bit error in every codeword corrected:", fixed == len(codewords) * 7, f"({fixed} cases)")
print("sphere-packing check: 2^4 codewords * (1 + 7 single-error patterns) =", 16 * 8, "= 2^7, so the Hamming code is perfect")

# --- the binary Golay code [23, 12, 7]: cyclic, generator polynomial g(x) = x^11 + x^10 + x^6 + x^5 + x^4 + x^2 + 1
G = 0b110001110101                                                       # 0xC75
def poly_mul(a, b):                                                       # carry-less multiplication over GF(2)
    out = 0
    while b:
        if b & 1: out ^= a
        a <<= 1; b >>= 1
    return out
def poly_mod(a, g):
    glen = g.bit_length()
    while a.bit_length() >= glen:
        a ^= g << (a.bit_length() - glen)
    return a
words = [poly_mul(m, G) for m in range(2 ** 12)]                          # every message polynomial times g(x) gives a codeword
print()
print("Golay code: codewords", len(set(words)), "= 2^12 | all have degree below 23:", max(w.bit_length() for w in words) <= 23)
distribution = Counter(weight(w) for w in words)
print("weight distribution:", dict(sorted(distribution.items())), "| minimum distance", min(w for w in distribution if w), "-> corrects up to 3 errors")
print("a codeword shifted cyclically stays a codeword (cyclic code):", all(poly_mod(((w << 1) | (w >> 22)) & (2 ** 23 - 1), G) == 0 for w in words[:500]))
print("sphere-packing:", sum(math.comb(23, i) for i in range(4)), "error patterns of weight <= 3, times 2^12 codewords =", sum(math.comb(23, i) for i in range(4)) * 2 ** 12, "= 2^23:", sum(math.comb(23, i) for i in range(4)) * 2 ** 12 == 2 ** 23, "-> the Golay code is perfect")

# --- syndrome decoding with a table: one entry per correctable error pattern
table = {}
for t in range(4):
    for positions in itertools.combinations(range(23), t):
        e = sum(1 << p for p in positions)
        table[poly_mod(e, G)] = e
print("syndromes of all error patterns of weight <= 3 are distinct:", len(table) == sum(math.comb(23, i) for i in range(4)), f"({len(table)} patterns, 2^11 = {2 ** 11} possible syndromes)")
correct = 0
trials = 3000
for _ in range(trials):
    sent = rng.choice(words)
    error = sum(1 << p for p in rng.sample(range(23), rng.randint(0, 3)))
    received = sent ^ error
    decoded = received ^ table[poly_mod(received, G)]
    correct += decoded == sent
print(f"decoding {trials} random codewords with 0 to 3 random errors: {correct} correct")
miscorrected = 0
for _ in range(trials):
    sent = rng.choice(words)
    received = sent ^ sum(1 << p for p in rng.sample(range(23), 4))
    miscorrected += (received ^ table[poly_mod(received, G)]) != sent
print(f"with 4 errors the decoder always lands on a different codeword (perfect code, no detection): {miscorrected} of {trials} wrong")

# --- random linear codes: the Gilbert-Varshamov bound says good codes exist, but it does not say how to decode them
def gv_guaranteed_distance(n, k):
    # largest d with sum_{i=0}^{d-2} C(n-1, i) < 2^(n-k): a linear [n, k, d] code exists
    d = 2
    while sum(math.comb(n - 1, i) for i in range(0, d - 1)) < 2 ** (n - k):
        d += 1
    return d - 1
print()
print("Gilbert-Varshamov: a binary linear [n, k, d] code exists whenever sum_{i=0}^{d-2} C(n-1, i) < 2^(n-k):")
for n, k in ((23, 12), (64, 32), (128, 64), (1024, 512)):
    d = gv_guaranteed_distance(n, k)
    print(f"[{n}, {k}]: a code with distance {d} is guaranteed, correcting {(d - 1) // 2} errors (rate {k / n:.2f})" + ("; the Golay code has distance 7 and does better than the guarantee" if n == 23 else ""))

For the Hamming code all 112 single-bit errors in all 16 codewords are corrected by reading the syndrome as a position, and 16 · 8 = 2^7 confirms perfection. For the Golay code the enumeration of all 4,096 codewords finds minimum distance 7 and the weight distribution 1, 253, 506, 1288, 1288, 506, 253, 1 (at weights 0, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 23); the sphere-packing identity (1 + 23 + 253 + 1771) · 2^12 = 2^23 holds exactly, so the code is perfect; the 2,048 syndromes of the error patterns of weight at most 3 are all distinct, and the table decoder corrected all 3,000 random words with up to 3 errors. With four errors it **always** decodes to a wrong codeword (3,000 of 3,000), which shows that a perfect code cannot even detect that decoding failed. The Gilbert-Varshamov lines show the guaranteed distance for random codes of rate one half, for instance distance 9 for [64, 32] and 116 for [1024, 512]; the Golay code (distance 7, the guarantee says 5) beats the guarantee because it is special.

**Takeaway for cryptography.** Decoding a code with a known structure is fast (a table, or the algebraic decoders of Goppa codes); decoding a random-looking linear code is a hard problem. A code-based scheme publishes a disguised version of a structured code, so that only the owner can decode quickly.

sections.title: 8.9 Syndrome Decoding
sections.summary: The decoding problem, Prange's information-set decoding implemented and compared with its predicted iteration count, and the same estimate for the Classic McEliece parameter sets with their public-key sizes reproduced from IR 8545.

blocks.markdown:
**Syndrome decoding**: given a parity-check matrix H (r × n), a syndrome s and a weight w, find an error vector e with H e = s and weight at most w. For random codes this problem is NP-hard in the worst case (a classical result by Berlekamp, McEliece and van Tilborg, cited from the literature), and the best known algorithms, the **information-set decoding (ISD)** family, are exponential even for the quantum versions (with a square-root speed-up of the search part). **Prange's algorithm**, the simplest ISD, guesses that all errors lie in a chosen set of r positions, solves the linear system restricted to those columns, and succeeds when the guess was right; the success probability per attempt is C(r, w)/C(n, w) times the probability (about 0.2888) that the restricted matrix is invertible. Better variants (Stern, Dumer, MMT, BJMM) reduce the cost by tens of bits at the same parameters.

The **McEliece** cryptosystem hides a structured code (a binary Goppa code with fast decoding) behind a random-looking parity-check matrix and publishes it; a legitimate receiver decodes quickly, an attacker faces syndrome decoding for a random-looking code. **Classic McEliece**, a KEM in the fourth NIST round (B94), uses this with parameters (n, m, t), where the code has length n, the field has degree m, and corrects t errors, so the check matrix has r = m·t rows. The listing runs Prange against random instances, compares the measured number of iterations with the prediction, and applies the formulas to the real parameter sets, whose public-key sizes are checked against IR 8545. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

The measured mean number of Prange iterations tracks the prediction 1/(p · 0.2888) closely (46.5 against 63.4, 139.2 against 131.1, 296.5 against 271.1 and 529.5 against 560.6 for the four sizes; the number of iterations is a geometric random variable, so a mean of 40 runs has a relative uncertainty of about 16 percent), while brute force would need hundreds of thousands to billions of steps, so ISD gains a rapidly growing factor. **Common mistakes:** quoting the Prange count as the security level; forgetting that the structured code must not be recoverable from the public matrix (the security of McEliece depends on the Goppa code looking random, an assumption); and ignoring the key size in protocol design (hybrid key exchange in TLS with a megabyte key is impractical, which is why ML-KEM is the standard choice for TLS).

sections.title: 8.10 Security Assumptions and Parameter Tradeoffs
sections.summary: A core-SVP primal-attack estimator that reproduces the shape of the ML-KEM parameter ladder, one-at-a-time parameter experiments, and an exact decryption-failure calculation validated by simulation.

blocks.markdown:
Every scheme in this module rests on an **assumption**: that a specific problem is hard. Lattice schemes assume LWE, SIS and their ring and module variants, hash-based schemes assume properties of the hash function, code-based schemes assume that decoding a random-looking code is hard. A **parameter set** picks sizes so that the best known attack costs at least the target (NIST categories 1, 3 and 5 correspond to the difficulty of breaking AES-128, -192 and -256 respectively), while keeping the decryption failure rate and the key and ciphertext sizes acceptable.

For lattice schemes the standard way to estimate the attack cost is the **primal attack** with BKZ lattice reduction. BKZ with block size β calls an SVP solver in dimension β and reaches the root Hermite factor δ(β) = ((πβ)^(1/β) · β/(2πe))^(1/(2(β−1))); the embedded vector (e, 1) is found when sqrt(β) · σ ≤ δ(β)^(2β − d − 1) · q^(m/d), with d = m + n + 1 and the number of samples m chosen to make β smallest. The **core-SVP** model then charges about 2^(0.292 β) operations classically and 2^(0.265 β) quantumly for the SVP call and ignores everything else. The listing implements this estimate, varies parameters one at a time, and then computes the **decryption failure probability** of a toy ring scheme exactly (by convolving probability distributions) and by simulation. The labs use Python with NumPy, plus the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py and dilithium-py (the same ones used in B10) as independent cross-checks. Everything runs on your own machine and every attack is mounted against toy parameters generated in the lesson. The toy schemes are for understanding only and must never protect real data.

import math
import numpy as np

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- part 1: a core-SVP style estimate of the primal attack on LWE
def delta_beta(b):
    # root Hermite factor reached by BKZ with block size b (the standard heuristic formula)
    return ((math.pi * b) ** (1 / b) * b / (2 * math.pi * math.e)) ** (1 / (2 * (b - 1)))

def primal_beta(n, q, sigma):
    # smallest block size b for which the unusually short vector (e, 1) is found: sqrt(b) * sigma <= delta_b^(2b - d - 1) * q^(m / d),
    # minimised over the number m of samples used, with d = m + n + 1 the dimension of the embedded lattice
    best = None
    for m in range(n, 3 * n + 1, max(1, n // 64)):
        d = m + n + 1
        for b in range(50, d):
            if math.sqrt(b) * sigma <= delta_beta(b) ** (2 * b - d - 1) * q ** (m / d):
                if best is None or b < best:
                    best = b
                break
    return best

def bits(b):
    return 0.292 * b, 0.265 * b                                           # classical and quantum sieving exponents used for core-SVP

print("primal-attack estimate for the three ML-KEM parameter sets (secret and error ~ centred binomial with eta1, so sigma^2 = eta1 / 2)")
print(f"{'parameter set':<12} {'secret length n*k':>18} {'eta1':>5} {'block size beta':>16} {'classical bits':>15} {'quantum bits':>13} {'NIST category':>14}")
for name, k, eta, category in (("ML-KEM-512", 2, 3, 1), ("ML-KEM-768", 3, 2, 3), ("ML-KEM-1024", 4, 2, 5)):
    b = primal_beta(256 * k, 3329, math.sqrt(eta / 2))
    c, qb = bits(b)
    print(f"{name:<12} {256 * k:>18} {eta:>5} {b:>16} {c:>15.1f} {qb:>13.1f} {category:>14}")
print("the estimate counts only the cost of one SVP call in dimension beta (the 'core-SVP' model): it ignores memory, the number of calls and known refinements,")
print("so it is a rough guide to the relative strength of the parameter sets, not a certified security level")

print()

print(f"{'change':<34} {'block size beta':>16} {'classical bits':>15}")

def row(label, **override):
    p = {**base, **override}
    b = primal_beta(256 * p["k"], p["q"], math.sqrt(p["eta"] / 2))
    print(f"{label:<34} {b:>16} {bits(b)[0]:>15.1f}")

row("module rank k = 3", k=3)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- part 2: the price of noise is decryption failure; exact calculation versus simulation
q, n, eta = 3329, 256, 32                                                  # an exaggerated noise width so that failures are frequent enough to measure
def cbd_pmf(eta):
    from math import comb
    binom = np.array([comb(eta, i) for i in range(eta + 1)], dtype=float) / 2 ** eta
    pmf = np.convolve(binom, binom[::-1])                                  # a - b with a, b ~ Binomial(eta, 1/2)
    return pmf, -eta                                                       # distribution over -eta..eta

pmf, lo = cbd_pmf(eta)
values = np.arange(lo, lo + len(pmf))
product = {}
for i, pi in enumerate(pmf):
    for j, pj in enumerate(pmf):
        v = int(values[i] * values[j])
        product[v] = product.get(v, 0.0) + pi * pj                           # distribution of a product of two independent centred-binomial values
lo_p, hi_p = min(product), max(product)
term = np.zeros(hi_p - lo_p + 1)
for v, pr in product.items():
    term[v - lo_p] = pr
size = 1 << 21
def power_by_fft(arr, offset, count):
    # distribution of the sum of `count` independent copies; the support starts at count * offset
    padded = np.zeros(size); padded[:len(arr)] = arr
    transform = np.fft.rfft(padded) ** count
    return np.fft.irfft(transform, size), count * offset
total, start = power_by_fft(term, lo_p, 2 * n)                              # e.r and s.e1 contribute 2n product terms in each coefficient
e2 = np.zeros(size); e2[:len(pmf)] = pmf
total = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(total) * np.fft.rfft(e2), size)
start += lo
support = np.arange(start, start + size)
total = np.clip(total, 0, None)
print()
print(f"toy ring-LWE with n = 256, q = 3329 and eta = {eta}: total probability mass of the noise distribution {total.sum():.6f}")
variance = float((total * support.astype(float) ** 2).sum())
print(f"exact standard deviation of the decryption noise {math.sqrt(variance):.1f} (formula sqrt(2 n (eta/2)^2 + eta/2) = {math.sqrt(2 * n * (eta / 2) ** 2 + eta / 2):.1f})")
def fails(noise_value, bit):
    x = (noise_value + bit * ((q + 1) // 2)) % q
    decoded = int(q // 4 < x < 3 * q // 4)
    return decoded != bit
exact = 0.0
for bit in (0, 1):
    mask = np.array([fails(int(v), bit) for v in support[np.abs(support) < 4 * q]])
    exact += 0.5 * float(total[np.abs(support) < 4 * q][mask].sum())
print(f"exact probability that one coefficient decrypts wrongly: {exact:.4f}")

def centred(size_):
    return rng.integers(0, 2, (size_, eta)).sum(1) - rng.integers(0, 2, (size_, eta)).sum(1)
def ring_mul(f, g):
    c = np.convolve(f, g); c = np.concatenate((c, np.zeros(2 * n - len(c), dtype=c.dtype)))
    return (c[:n] - c[n:]) % q
a = rng.integers(0, q, n)
wrong = count = 0

    b_ = (ring_mul(a, s_) + e_) % q
    u = (ring_mul(a, r_) + e1_) % q
    message = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
    v = (ring_mul(b_, r_) + e2_ + ((q + 1) // 2) * message) % q
    x = (v - ring_mul(s_, u)) % q
    decoded = ((x > q // 4) & (x < 3 * q // 4)).astype(int)
    wrong += int((decoded != message).sum()); count += n
print(f"simulation of the real toy scheme: {wrong} wrong coefficients out of {count:,} = {wrong / count:.4f}")
print("for the real ML-KEM sets the same method (with compression included) gives the failure rates of FIPS 203, Table 1: 2^-138.8, 2^-164.8 and 2^-174.8")

blocks.markdown:
The estimator gives block sizes 406, 625 and 878 for the three ML-KEM sets, so core-SVP costs of about 2^119, 2^183 and 2^256 classically (2^108, 2^166 and 2^233 quantumly), a ladder that rises with the NIST category: 1, 3 and 5. These values are in the range of the published analyses of Kyber that I remember (not re-read here, so treat the comparison as unverified), and the estimate is a deliberately simple model: it ignores the memory cost of sieving, the polynomial overhead, the dual attack and a number of refinements, so it indicates relative strength and does not certify an absolute level. The one-at-a-time experiments show the tradeoffs. Raising the module rank from 2 to 3 to 4 raises β from 406 to 661 and 925. Narrower noise (η = 1) lowers β to 346, wider noise (η = 6) raises it to 452, but wider noise also raises the decryption failure probability, which is the correctness price of 8.2. A smaller modulus raises the hardness at the same noise (q = 1000 gives 492) because the noise is relatively larger, while a modulus like ML-DSA's 8,380,417 with the same small noise would be very weak (β = 155): the *ratio* of modulus to noise width is what matters, and signatures use a larger modulus with correspondingly larger secrets and different bounds.

The failure calculation shows the method of the standard. For the toy with η = 32 the exact distribution gives a per-coefficient failure probability of 0.0217 (standard deviation of the noise 362.1, equal to the closed form), and the simulation of the actual toy scheme measures 0.0214. FIPS 203 Table 1 lists 2^-138.8, 2^-164.8 and 2^-174.8 for the three real sets, obtained by the same kind of calculation with the compression noise included (the toy has no compression). **Why failure probability matters:** the CCA transform of ML-KEM (B9) assumes that honestly generated ciphertexts essentially never fail, because a failure is observable and can leak information about the secret key.

**Honest limits.** None of this proves security. Security estimates are statements about the *best known* attacks, and they have been revised before (for instance by new cost models for sieving and by new attack techniques), so standards add margin and the community keeps analysing. A reasoned position: lattice assumptions are well studied but structured variants add an assumption; hash-based signatures rest on the least; and code-based schemes have the longest analysis history but the largest keys.
